lead: Virtualization is classified by the implementation level: the place where the software layer sits between a program and the resources it uses. The layer may be inside one application, in a library, in the operating system, or directly on the hardware. This taxonomy exists because each level trades portability, isolation, and overhead differently. A phone user sees it through app runtimes and containers; a data centre sees it through hypervisors.
prereq: You need: 3.1, where virtualization inserts a software layer that shares one physical machine among isolated virtual machines.

blocks.text: Every virtual system has an interface. Below the interface, resources are real or already virtual. Above it, a program believes it owns a machine. The implementation level names that interface. Put the layer just above the hardware and you can run whole operating systems. Put it inside one process and you can run bytecode on any host. The classification tells you what is shared and what is emulated.

Two other views appear in exams. A resource-based view asks what is virtualized: CPU, memory, storage, or network. A transparency-based view asks how much the guest knows about the layer. These are useful tags, not separate rungs on the same ladder. Some syllabi call the whole idea the taxonomy of virtualization techniques, or types of virtualization.

The levels are application, library, operating-system, and hardware. The order runs from a layer close to one program to a layer close to the hardware. The hardware branch later splits by guest cooperation into full and para virtualization, covered in 3.4. The operating-system branch leads to containers in 3.7.
Each level answers a different need.

items: Application-level. A virtual machine runs as an ordinary process on the host operating system. It executes portable bytecode, which is code for a virtual processor. The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) runs Java bytecode; the Common Language Runtime (CLR) runs .NET code. No guest operating system boots, and no hypervisor is involved. The benefit is portability: the same bytecode runs on any host with a compatible runtime.

Library-level. The layer replaces or translates calls to a library or application programming interface (API). WINE lets many Windows programs run on Linux by implementing Windows library calls with Linux calls. The program still runs on the host operating system. Only programs that use the translated calls work, so coverage is partial.

Operating-system level. One host kernel is shared by many isolated user-space instances. Containers use namespaces (which make resources look private to a process group) and cgroups (which cap resource use); details are in 3.7. Each container looks like a small server, but it has no kernel of its own. Startup is fast and overhead is low because the kernel is not duplicated.

Hardware level. A hypervisor, also called a virtual machine monitor, sits between the physical hardware and one or more guest operating systems. It exports virtual hardware: virtual CPUs, memory, disks, and network cards. The guest OS boots on that virtual hardware. The hypervisor is covered in 3.3. Hardware level splits into full and para by how much the guest cooperates, not by a new level.

blocks.text: A system can mix levels. A container can run a JVM; a hypervisor can host a VM that runs Docker.

sections.h3: Reading a system by its level

blocks.text: Use four questions in order. The first match gives the level.

items: Ask whether a guest operating system boots on virtual hardware. If yes, the level is hardware-level.

Ask whether one host kernel runs several isolated user-space environments, each looking like a separate server, with no kernel image of its own (namespaces and cgroups). If yes, the level is OS-level.
Ask whether a runtime executes portable code as an ordinary process. If yes, the level is application-level.
Ask whether library or API calls are translated for a foreign program. If yes, the level is library-level.

blocks.text: A JVM or a WINE program is an ordinary host process; it shares the kernel but is not an isolated user-space environment, so it does not match the OS-level test.

The order matters. A container running a Java service is OS-level for the container and application-level for the JVM inside it. Name the layer you are asked about, not every layer present. Level is also separate from transparency. Full and para are choices inside hardware-level virtualization: full hides the hypervisor from an unmodified guest; para expects a modified guest to make hypercalls, which are calls into the hypervisor. Both are hardware-level because both run a guest OS on virtual hardware.

figure.caption: Ask the four questions in order; the first yes names the level. Xen answers yes to the first question, so it stops at hardware-level and full virtualization.

spec.aria: A flowchart of four ordered questions classifies Xen as hardware-level and full, Docker as OS-level, the JVM as application-level, and WINE as library-level.

examples.question: A cloud team runs four workloads. Workload X: Xen with an unmodified guest operating system. Workload D: Docker containers on one Linux host. Workload J: a Java program on the JVM. Workload W: a Windows program under WINE on Linux. Classify each workload by implementation level. For the Xen workload, state which split inside hardware-level virtualization applies.
steps: Xen: the hypervisor sits between the hardware and the guest OS and exports virtual hardware. The guest OS boots on that virtual hardware, so the level is hardware-level. The guest is unmodified, so the transparency choice is full virtualization; see 3.4.
Docker: containers share the host Linux kernel and isolate processes with namespaces and cgroups. No guest OS boots, so the level is OS-level; see 3.7.
JVM: the Java Virtual Machine runs as an ordinary process on the host OS and executes Java bytecode. The level is application-level.
WINE: WINE translates Windows library calls into Linux calls for a program running on the host OS. The level is library-level.
examples.answer: Xen is hardware-level (full virtualization); Docker is OS-level; the JVM is application-level; WINE is library-level.

traps: Level is not the same as full or para. Full and para are transparency choices inside hardware-level virtualization.
Application-level virtual machines such as the JVM are not hypervisor virtual machines. They run as processes and do not boot a guest OS.
Library-level virtualization translates calls; it does not virtualize hardware. WINE is not a hypervisor.
OS-level virtualization shares the host kernel. A container has no guest kernel, so calling it a full virtual machine is wrong.
A mixed system has several levels. State which layer the question asks about; a container running a JVM is both OS-level and application-level depending on the boundary.

quiz.q: Name the four implementation levels of virtualization used in this taxonomy.
quiz.a: Application, library, operating-system, and hardware level.

quiz.q: Why is the JVM application-level and not hardware-level?
quiz.a: The JVM runs as a normal process on the host OS and executes bytecode. It does not boot a guest OS on virtual hardware, and no hypervisor sits below it.

quiz.q: Classify: (a) a Linux process isolated with namespaces and cgroups, (b) a .NET program on the CLR, (c) WINE running a Windows application on Linux, (d) Xen running an unmodified FreeBSD guest.

Two systems both run guest operating systems on virtual hardware. System A runs unmodified Windows; System B runs a modified Linux that uses hypercalls. Are they at different implementation levels? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Both are hardware-level. System A is full virtualization; System B is para-virtualization. Full and para describe guest transparency, not level.

quiz.q: What does library-level virtualization reuse, and what does it not provide?
quiz.a: It reuses the host OS and translates library or API calls. It does not provide a guest OS or virtual hardware, and it works only for programs that use the translated calls.

quiz.q: A vendor says Docker gives full virtualization because each container looks like a separate server. Correct the statement.
quiz.a: Docker is OS-level. Containers share the host kernel and isolate processes with namespaces and cgroups. Full virtualization is a hardware-level choice for an unmodified guest OS on a hypervisor.

quiz.q: A team wants many isolated web servers on one Linux host with low startup delay. Which implementation level fits, and which later section gives the mechanism?
quiz.a: OS-level virtualization fits: containers share the kernel and start fast. The mechanism is in 3.7.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry now blends levels: microVMs such as Firecracker give hardware-level isolation with container-like startup, and sandboxed runtimes such as gVisor intercept system calls in user space. Unikernels compile an application with a minimal kernel. Kata Containers wraps containers in lightweight VMs. Search for microVM, unikernel, gVisor, and Kata Containers to see how the taxonomy bends.
